section_summary: This section covers monthly political reports and accompanying schedules of despatches and telegrams transmitted by the American Embassy in Tokyo to the Department of State between July and December 1930. Major political developments include the contentious Privy Council ratification of the London Naval Treaty, cabinet friction leading to naval leadership changes, the attempted assassination of Prime Minister Osachi Hamaguchi by an Aikokusha nationalist, resulting governmental instability, and the tumultuous opening of the 59th Imperial Diet. The dispatches also record widespread economic depression, deflation following the lifting of the gold embargo, agrarian distress and falling rice prices, industrial curtailment, communist crackdowns, the indigenous Musha uprising in Taiwan, and catastrophic natural disasters including the Izu earthquake.

subfiles.about: Continuation of the monthly political report for July 1930 and accompanying schedules of despatches and telegrams sent to the Department.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This concluding portion of the July 1930 political report discusses the Minseito government's retrenchment policy, budgetary cuts across ministries, and agrarian relief efforts prompted by falling cocoon prices and debts. It highlights controversies surrounding teachers' salary reductions, urban unemployed laborers returning to rural villages, and the popular 'Use Home Products' (Kokusan Ai-yo) campaign. It also reports the submission of the London Naval Treaty to the Emperor, location debates over the Showa Steel Works between Anshan and Shin Gishu, and the death of Field Marshal Count Yasukata Oku. Appended are complete lists of Embassy despatches (Nos. 189–218) and telegrams (Nos. 113–127) sent during July 1930.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 219: Political Report for July, 1930

subfiles.about: Monthly political report for August 1930 transmitting Report No. 47 on domestic affairs, aviation, labor politics, and foreign relations.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Chargé Neville transmits the August report, which opens with a discussion of the popular cultural craze surrounding Townsend Harris and his maidservant Okichi, commemorated by songs, films, and a new Tokyo shrine. The report details successful flights by Japanese aviators Yoshiwara and Azuma alongside Harold Bromley and Harold Gatty's aborted transpacific attempt from Kasumigaura. Diplomatic and internal friction are reviewed, including Soviet harassment of the Bank of Chosen in Vladivostok, schisms within the radical Farmer-Labor Party, the trial of forty-four communists in Karafuto, and Cabinet approval of a 40-million-yen agrarian relief loan. Appended are complete lists of Embassy despatches (Nos. 219–243) and telegrams (Nos. 128–150) transmitted during August 1930.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 245: Report of Conditions in Japan During the Month of August, 1930 (Report No. 47)

subfiles.about: Monthly political report for September 1930 transmitting Report No. 48 detailing Privy Council approval of the London Naval Treaty and domestic economic trends.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes reviews September developments under the theme of 'rejuvenation,' highlighting the Privy Council's sudden reversal on September 17 to recommend ratification of the London Naval Treaty. The report covers the public corruption trial of former Chosen Governor General Yamanashi, the 19th International Statistical Conference held in Tokyo, preparations for the second decennial census, and the launch of the Association for the Use of Home Products. It also analyzes extensive industrial production curtailments across cotton spinning, silk, and cement manufacturing despite official claims of early business recovery. Appended are schedules of Embassy despatches (Nos. 244–252 and 1–13) and telegrams (Nos. 151–181) dispatched during September 1930.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 20: Report of Conditions in Japan During the Month of September 1930 (Report No. 48)

subfiles.about: Monthly political report for October 1930 transmitting Report No. 49 covering treaty approval, naval resignations, financial loans, and colonial unrest.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes reports on the conclusion of the second decennial national census and the Privy Council's plenary adoption of the London Naval Treaty, which precipitated the resignation of Navy Minister Admiral Takarabe and the appointment of Admiral Abo. The report reviews the violent uprising of aborigines in central Taiwan, negotiations with J. P. Morgan & Co. for a 45-million-yen Taiwan Power Company foreign loan, and underwriting of corporate debentures by insurance syndicates. It highlights rising unemployment (378,500), a catastrophic drop in rice prices that prompted government purchase and tariff increases, and extensive personnel changes among senior Japanese diplomats. Concluding pages list despatches (Nos. 14–36) and telegrams (Nos. 182–204) sent during October 1930.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 38: Report of Conditions in Japan During the Month of October, 1930 (Report No. 49)

subfiles.about: Monthly political report for November 1930 transmitting Report No. 50 detailing the attempted assassination of Premier Hamaguchi and multiple domestic crises.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: The report details a succession of major shocks in Japan, beginning with the total destruction by fire of the American-owned newspaper Japan Advertiser on November 4. On November 14, Prime Minister Osachi Hamaguchi was shot and critically wounded at Tokyo Station by Tomeo Sagoya, an operative of the reactionary Aikokusha, leading to Baron Shidehara assuming interim premiership duties. It describes the destructive Izu earthquake of November 26 centered near Mishima which claimed some 250 lives, mass dismissals of 2,500 workers at Mitsubishi dockyards, a dramatic 130-hour chimney-sitting strike settlement in Kawasaki, May Day communist violence at Inage Shrine, bumper rice crop measures, and the solo flight visit of British aviator Mrs. Victor Bruce. Appended are lists of Embassy despatches (Nos. 37–67) and telegrams (Nos. 205–233) transmitted during November 1930.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 74: Report of Conditions in Japan During the Month of November, 1930 (Report No. 50)

subfiles.about: Monthly political report for December 1930 transmitting Report No. 51 covering the political fallout of the Premier's incapacitation, Diet convocation, and budget proposals.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes reports on the successful passing of year-end bill settlements aided by Industrial Bank credit, alongside persistent political turmoil due to Premier Hamaguchi's inability to resume official duties. Legal and political developments include the indictment of Aikokusha associates Yoshikatsu Matsuki and Ainosuke Iwata, a united press revolt against police censorship, and corruption convictions of former Education Minister Kazuta Kobashi and Vice Minister Sango Satake in the Echigo Railway scandal. It reviews the convocation of the 59th Imperial Diet, the Seiyukai opposition's alternative economic platform, the draft 1931–1932 national budget, colonial budgets, the Soviet closure of the Bank of Chosen's Vladivostok branch, and Sino-Japanese wireless negotiations. The subfile concludes with lists of Embassy despatches (Nos. 68–96) and telegrams (Nos. 234–257) sent during December 1930.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 107: Report of Conditions in Japan During the Month of December, 1930 (Report No. 51)
